newsitem.title: USA: IMF says currency misalignments not more common.
newsitem.headline: IMF says currency misalignments not more common.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund does not think that major currency misalignments that can threaten the monetary system are more common now than in the past when capital markets were less integrated, a senior official said Monday.

In a briefing for reporters durint the IMF/World Bank spring meetings, Flemming Larsen, deputy director of the IMF's research department, said that neither increased volatility nor currency misalignments where the markets stray far from economic fundamentals are happening more now.
He said the IMF worries about the misalignments because of the damage they can do to the system when dramatic corrections suddenly occur.
"In such a situation, you have the potential for large sudden changes in sentiment ... that can have serious adverse consequences for the international monetary system," he said.
But he said so far there was no indication that this is a growing problem although it would be "naive to believe that they can be avoided altogether."

He said the most recent case was the very significant appreciation of the yen in the spring of 1995." At the time, (we) felt (the appreciation ) had gone way beyond what could be explained by, or justified by the fundamentals," he said.
Larsen said it clearly helped prolong the serious weakness if not recession in the Japanese economy in recent years.
"(It) will remain a major challenge to identify such episodes and to reach a consensus on what can be done when they arise," he said.
Larsen spoke at a briefing for reporters on the impact of globalization in which the world's economies are closely tied together by both trade and financial flows.

He also said there was no evidence that the earnings inequality between skilled and unskilled workers in the United States reflected increased trade with developing countries, as has sometimes been alleged.
